sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the author draws practical consequences from the recipients' rebirth: they must strip off relational vices, crave the pure word, and grow toward a salvation that is not yet complete but is the destination of an ongoing journey.
sections.relevance: The passage presents salvation as something the recipients must actively grow toward rather than a settled, unilaterally determined outcome. The imperative 'rid yourselves' treats moral transformation as requiring genuine human participation. The command to 'long for the pure milk of the word' assumes the recipients' desire and effort are real factors in their spiritual development. The neutral reading explicitly states that 'salvation, in the author's understanding, is not a completed event but something toward which the recipients are growing,' with the word's nourishment enabling the journey. This framing implies human agency as a genuine component of the salvific process -- growth toward salvation can stall if the recipients fail to strip off vices or fail to feed on the word.
key_phrases: rid yourselves of all malice and all deceit
long for the pure milk of the word
so that by it you may grow in respect to salvation

sections.section_title: The Living Stone and the Spiritual House
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the author develops a building metaphor in which Christ is a living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, and the recipients who come to him are also living stones being built into a spiritual house for a holy priesthood that offers spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ.

The neutral reading finds that the author chains three Old Testament stone texts (Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22, Isaiah 8:14) to establish that the same stone -- Christ -- produces opposite effects depending on the human response: honor for those who believe and stumbling for those who disobey, with the causal connection made explicit ('they stumble because they are disobedient to the word').
sections.relevance: 1 Peter 2:8 ('they stumble... as they were destined to do') is conventionally cited as proof that God predestines certain individuals to disobedience and damnation. The neutral reading reveals the passage is about something else. The author states the cause of stumbling explicitly: 'they stumble because they are disobedient to the word' -- disobedience is presented as the people's own act, not something imposed on them. The phrase 'to this they were also appointed' (eis ho kai etethesan) is grammatically ambiguous, but the neutral reading favors the interpretation that God appointed the consequence structure -- that the stone would function as both cornerstone and stumbling block -- not that God appointed specific individuals to disobey. The neutral reading states: 'God placed the stone; those who disobey it fall over it. The placement of the stone was God's appointment; the disobedience is the people's own.' The concluding summary is decisive: 'The stone is one; the responses to it are two... The difference lies entirely in how people respond to it.' This is consistent with the Isaiah 8:14 source text, where God's becoming a stumbling stone results from Israel's refusal to fear God properly, not from arbitrary imposition.
key_phrases: the one who believes in Him will not be put to shame
they stumble because they are disobedient to the word
to this they were also appointed
The stone is one; the responses to it are two
The difference lies entirely in how people respond to it

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the author applies four titles drawn from Old Testament texts describing Israel (chosen people, royal priesthood, holy nation, God's own possession) to the recipients, states their vocation is outward proclamation of God's excellencies, and frames their experience through the Hosea reversal: those who were 'not a people' are now 'the people of God.'
sections.relevance: The election language here is corporate and vocational, not individual and soteriological. The neutral reading identifies every phrase as drawn from texts about Israel's collective covenant identity and national vocation. The Exodus 19:5-6 source text, as the neutral reading explicitly notes, was conditional: 'if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, then you shall be My own possession.' The identity was 'contingent on obedience,' and 'Israel's history, as told in the prophets, is the story of the repeated failure to maintain this covenant obedience.' The purpose of the election is proclamation ('so that you may proclaim the excellencies'), a vocational calling to service rather than an irresistible decree of individual salvation. The Hosea reversal concerns a real change in communal status that presupposes response to the gospel. The word ethnos ('nation') applied to the community is constituted 'not by ethnicity or geography but by God's calling and their response to it' -- the neutral reading names both divine calling and human response as constitutive.
key_phrases: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession
so that you may proclaim the excellencies
if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant
not by ethnicity or geography but by God's calling and their response to it
you once were not a people, but now you are the people of God

sections.section_title: The Exile's Conduct Among the Nations
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the author exhorts the recipients as foreigners and strangers to abstain from fleshly lusts that 'wage war against the soul' and to maintain visibly excellent behavior among the Gentiles so that outsiders who slander them will ultimately glorify God.
sections.relevance: The military metaphor -- fleshly lusts 'wage war against the soul' -- implies a genuine conflict with a non-predetermined outcome. The neutral reading connects 'soul' to 1:9 ('the salvation of your souls') and 1:22 ('you have purified your souls'), identifying the soul as 'what is being saved' and 'what has been purified.' The command to abstain treats human resistance as a real factor: if the outcome were unilaterally determined, warning about an active siege against the thing being saved would be incoherent. The recipients must genuinely fight to protect what God is working to deliver.
key_phrases: abstain from fleshly lusts
which wage war against the soul
keep your behavior excellent among the Gentiles

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the author instructs the community to submit to human governing institutions for the Lord's sake, to silence ignorant critics through good conduct, to exercise their freedom as bond-servants of God, and to honor all people while fearing God alone.

The neutral reading finds that the author instructs household servants to submit to their masters -- including harsh ones -- and distinguishes between suffering deserved as punishment for sin (which earns no credit) and suffering unjustly while maintaining consciousness of God (which finds favor with God).

sections.section_title: The Example and Work of Christ in Suffering
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Christ's suffering is presented as both exemplary (a pattern the community traces) and redemptive (bearing sins so that they might die to sin and live for righteousness), with the recipients described as formerly straying sheep who have now returned to the Shepherd and Guardian of their souls.
sections.relevance: Two features of the neutral reading bear on the determinism question. First, Christ's redemptive work creates possibility but does not automatically produce the outcome: the neutral reading states that 'the death to sin is not automatic; it is the purpose (hina) of Christ's bearing of sins,' and that 'the community's ethical conduct is grounded in Christ's work, not in mere willpower.' Christ's work is necessary but the community must actively follow in his steps, entrust themselves to the righteous judge, and trace the pattern he left. Second, the recipients' conversion is described using epistrepho, 'the standard LXX word for repentance -- turning back to God.' The neutral reading initially calls their conversion 'a homecoming: sheep who were wandering have found their way back,' then qualifies: 'or rather, have been found and brought back.' Both human turning and divine retrieval are present, but the use of the repentance verb implies genuine human agency in the return, while Christ's shepherding implies divine initiative. Neither is excluded.
key_phrases: leaving you an example, so that you would follow in His steps
the death to sin is not automatic; it is the purpose of Christ's bearing of sins
you have returned to the Shepherd and Guardian of your souls
kept entrusting Himself to Him who judges righteously
